**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Decode and return RFC dynamic-registration fields**

When an OAuth or MCP client follows the advertised `registration_endpoint`, it sends RFC dynamic-registration fields such as `client_name`, `redirect_uris`, and string-valued `scope`; decoding directly into this untagged engine struct with `DisallowUnknownFields` rejects that request. Even clients using the private camel-case shape receive `ID` rather than the required `client_id`, so conforming clients cannot complete registration. Add dedicated RFC-compatible HTTP request and response DTOs around the engine model.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Prune expired state before applying capacity limits**

In the durable store, expired but never consumed authorization, consent, and code rows fail this `consumed_at IS NOT NULL` predicate, while refresh-grant rows are never considered at all. Capacity checks count every historical row and admission does not invoke pruning, so 1,024 abandoned authorization attempts or 4,096 ordinary refresh rotations can permanently force subsequent operations to return capacity errors even after all relevant TTLs expire. Remove expired transient rows and whole refresh families after family expiry, atomically before admission.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Derive advertised endpoints from the configured issuer**

When TLS is terminated by a reverse proxy, `r.TLS` is nil and `r.Host` is commonly an internal host, so metadata declares the configured public issuer but advertises HTTP/internal authorization, token, registration, revocation, and JWKS endpoints. Clients then fail issuer validation or cannot reach those endpoints; an untrusted Host header can also poison discovery and registration `Location` values. Resolve endpoint paths against `Config.Issuer` instead of request transport fields.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve arbitrary PrincipalCodec byte output**

If a consumer supplies a versioned, encrypted, gob, or otherwise non-JSON codec permitted by the `PrincipalCodec` byte-slice contract, converting its output to `json.RawMessage` makes the enclosing `json.Marshal` reject the payload as invalid JSON. Login completion or later grant persistence then fails even though the codec itself succeeded. Store the encoded data as an ordinary `[]byte` so JSON base64-encodes it, or explicitly constrain and validate the codec contract as JSON.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Apply HTTPPolicy limits before parsing form bodies**

When `MaxBodyBytes` is below `net/http`'s built-in form limit—as it is with the default 1 MiB policy—token requests bypass the configured bound because `ParseForm` is called without first wrapping the body in `http.MaxBytesReader`; the consent and revocation handlers do the same. An unauthenticated caller can therefore make each endpoint read and allocate for bodies up to the larger library default, and the configured array limit is likewise unused for consent scopes. Apply the policy before parsing and validate field and array sizes consistently.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Bind revalidation output to the original subject**

When a `PrincipalRevalidator` mistakenly returns `RevalidationEligible` with a different valid subject, the engine uses that principal to issue the access token and persist the successor grant without checking it against `grant.Principal.Subject`. This turns an adapter lookup/cache error into a cross-account authorization grant; reject eligible results whose returned subject is empty or differs from the subject being revalidated.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Redirect trusted authorization errors back to the client**

Once the client and exact registered redirect URI have been validated, failures such as an unsupported resource or invalid scope still take this branch and return a JSON error directly to the browser. The OAuth client therefore never receives its callback or the original `state`, leaving the authorization attempt hanging; the engine/transport needs to distinguish pre-validation failures from errors that can safely be redirected with `error` and `state` parameters.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Validate every operational policy limit**

A manually constructed `Config` can pass validation while limits such as `MaxRefreshGrants`, `MaxAuthorizations`, `MaxConsents`, `MaxDisplayName`, or `MaxFieldBytes` are zero or negative. For example, setting the currently checked fields positive but leaving `MaxRefreshGrants` at zero lets `New` succeed, after which every code exchange fails the store's `count >= MaxRefreshGrants` check with a capacity error. Validate all limits consumed by the engine and stores so accepted configurations remain usable.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Allow query components in exact redirect URIs**

Dynamic registration rejects every redirect URI containing a query because `validOrigin` disallows `RawQuery`, even though `NewRedirectURI` permits queries and the redirect response logic preserves them. Clients whose fixed callback is something like `https://client.example/callback?tenant=a` consequently cannot register despite exact-string redirect matching being sufficient to bind it; reserve the no-query restriction for issuer/resource origins rather than redirect URIs.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Recognize the IPv6 loopback hostname without brackets**

For an HTTP loopback redirect such as `http://[::1]:8080/callback`, `url.URL.Hostname()` returns `::1` with the brackets removed, so comparison with `"[::1]"` always fails. Native clients listening on the standard IPv6 loopback address therefore cannot register or authorize; compare the hostname to `"::1"`.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

## CodeQL / Open URL redirect

This path to an untrusted URL redirection depends on a [user-provided value](1).

[Show more details](https://github.com/go-go-golems/oh-auth/security/code-scanning/1)

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Make the dynamic-client capacity recoverable**

Because `/oauth/register` is unauthenticated, an attacker can submit the default 256 valid registrations and permanently trigger this capacity branch. The repository has no client deletion operation, `pruneTx` never removes clients, and `TouchClient` is never invoked, so unlike the transient-state quotas, this limit can never recover without manually modifying the database. Add a client lifecycle/eviction mechanism or otherwise protect registration before enforcing a lifetime count.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Propagate refresh-family revocation failures**

When revalidation reports an ineligible principal and SQLite cannot persist the family revocation, this ignored error still returns `invalid_grant` even though the refresh token remains active. If revalidation later reports the principal eligible again, that same token can successfully refresh; return a temporary error when revocation fails and report `invalid_grant` only after the family is durably revoked.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Resolve consent URLs against the configured issuer**

When the configured issuer contains a path, which `Config.Validate` currently accepts, metadata advertises endpoints under that path but login completion redirects to the host-root `/oauth/consent`. For example, issuer `https://auth.example/base` advertises `/base/oauth/authorize` yet sends the browser to `/oauth/consent`, where the flow will normally 404; the consent form also hardcodes the root path. Have the HTTP transport resolve the consent destination and form action against the configured issuer or mount prefix.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Remove the dangling registration Location**

Every successful registration advertises a created-resource URL under `/oauth/register/{client_id}`, but `Mount` only registers the exact `/oauth/register` endpoint and there is no registration-management handler anywhere in the repository. Clients that follow the 201 `Location` therefore receive a 404; either implement the advertised resource or omit the header.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Revoke consumed refresh families before external work**

When a previously rotated refresh token is replayed with the correct client ID, `grant.ConsumedAt` is ignored here and replay detection is deferred to `CommitRefreshRotation`. If revalidation returns an error or `Unknown`, or resource lookup, scope evaluation, token issuance, or secret generation fails first, the commit is never reached and the active successor family is not revoked despite confirmed reuse of a consumed credential. Handle `ConsumedAt` immediately after loading and validating the grant, durably revoking the family before invoking fallible adapters.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve clients with live refresh grants**

When an unverified client has not started a new authorization for `UnverifiedClientTTL` but still has an unexpired refresh family, the next registration deletes the client because this exclusion checks only live authorization rows. Refresh activity never calls `TouchClient`, so the existing grant can continue rotating while every subsequent authorization fails at `GetClient`; either treat live refresh families as child state that prevents eviction or renew the client lease during token activity.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Stop advertising unsupported OpenID discovery**

Clients probing this standard OpenID Connect discovery path receive apparently valid metadata even though the repository has no OpenID scope, ID-token issuance, UserInfo endpoint, or the required OIDC discovery fields. Such clients can select this server as an OIDC provider and only fail later in the authorization flow; expose only the OAuth authorization-server metadata endpoint unless OIDC is actually implemented.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Advertise the supported token authentication method**

For discovery-driven clients, omitting `token_endpoint_auth_methods_supported` means the standards-defined default is `client_secret_basic`, but this token endpoint only accepts public-client identification through the form body and does not parse HTTP Basic credentials. Clients that rely on metadata can therefore choose an authentication method the server cannot handle; advertise `none` explicitly.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P1 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P1-orange?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Separate refresh admission from retained generations**

With the default global limit of 4,096, every successful rotation adds a row while consumed generations remain until the family expires, so one rapidly rotated grant—or ordinary traffic across many clients—can make all subsequent code exchanges and refreshes return capacity errors for up to the 30-day refresh lifetime. The new family-expiry pruning is fresh evidence that the earlier capacity issue remains: it deliberately retains every generation of every live family. Bound replay-history storage separately and base grant admission on active families/current grants so retained generations cannot exhaust the global operational quota.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Preserve clients referenced by consent and code state**

When a valid configuration sets `UnverifiedClientTTL` below `ConsentTTL` or `CodeTTL`, completing login consumes the authorization and leaves no refresh grant yet; a concurrent registration can then delete the client even though its consent session or authorization code is still live. The fresh lifecycle query now protects live authorizations and refresh grants but still omits both consent and code rows, allowing the existing flow to exchange its snapshot-backed code into a refresh grant for a client that no longer exists and making later authorizations fail. Include every live child-state table in the exclusion or validate a TTL ordering that makes this impossible.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Accept additional dynamic-registration metadata**

The updated registration DTO is fresh evidence that the earlier registration fix remains incomplete: `DisallowUnknownFields` still rejects conforming requests containing standard optional or extension metadata such as `client_uri`, `contacts`, or `software_id`, because none of those fields exist in the DTO. Registration clients that routinely include such metadata therefore receive `invalid_client_metadata`; accept the standard fields or safely ignore metadata the server does not use.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Generate client IDs through a compatible secret method**

When an application provides a valid custom `SecretSource` whose transaction tokens use ordinary base64 characters such as `+`, `/`, or `=`, `NewTransactionToken` can return them successfully but `NewClientID` rejects them because client IDs use a narrower character set. Every dynamic registration then fails with a 503 even though the secret source satisfies its interface; add a dedicated client-ID generator or encode generated bytes into the client-ID alphabet.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Derive the displayed authorization end from grant creation**

The consent page claims authorization ends at `consent.ExpiresAt + RefreshTTL`, but the refresh grant actually expires at `codeExchangeTime + RefreshTTL`. Approving immediately makes the displayed deadline almost a full consent TTL later than reality, while approving near consent expiry and delaying code exchange can make the real grant outlive the displayed deadline; bind the grant to the disclosed deadline or avoid presenting this value as the actual authorization end.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Return distinct statuses for media-type and size failures**

When a token request has an unsupported `Content-Type` or exceeds `MaxBodyBytes`, `parseForm` exposes both conditions through `err`, but this branch converts every failure to a 400 `invalid_request`. Consequently clients and intermediaries cannot distinguish malformed OAuth parameters from an unsupported representation or an oversized payload; preserve these error categories and return 415 and 413 respectively. The registration, consent, and revocation handlers currently collapse the same conditions in the same way.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.

**<sub><sub>![P2 Badge](https://img.shields.io/badge/P2-yellow?style=flat)</sub></sub>  Reject colliding refresh-token digests before rotation**

When a custom or faulty `SecretSource` returns a refresh token whose digest is already present, this assignment silently overwrites that grant after consuming the current generation. A collision with another family transfers the raw token to a different grant, while a collision with the current digest makes rotation return the same reusable credential and defeats replay detection. The SQLite store reports `ErrConflict`, and the memory store should perform the same existence check before mutating either record; its code-exchange path has the same unchecked map assignment.

Useful? React with 👍 / 👎.
